subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria) moved:
subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
Thai, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived in the commercial and industrial development of the province of Nova Scotia when the Intercolonial railway bf Canada should be extended into the nonrailway counties of the eastern section of that province.
He said: This is not at all a new subject to this House, nor to certain sections of the country; still it is so important, particularly to the part of the country from which 1 come, that it is desirable, in my judgment, to bring it once more to the attention of the government and of hon. members of this House. To a person as well acquainted with the circumstances and conditions in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia as I am myself, the proposition contained in this resolution is self-evident, that is, that the time has arrived when this great railway, the Intercolonial, should extend itself into the portions of the province of Nova Scotia which now have no railway lacilities. It is also self-evident to every business man, and particularly so to the business man of to-day, that railway transportation which is, perhaps, the only up-to-date method of transportation, is essential to the very life and proper development of any country. That is particularly the case in a province like Nova Scotia, or any other country where we have not water carriage all the time. It may be said that, in countries where transportation by water is open at all times of the year, railway facilities are not so essential; but to us jn the province of Nova Scotia where we can carry goods by water only for half of the year, railway facilities are indispensable to the success of the country. The use that people make of these facilities when placed at their disposal is entirely for themselves, that is the way in which the people husband and improve the facilities within their reach is entirely a matter for themselves. But while that is the case, there are some responsibilities devolving upon the government of the day as to what facilities, what improvements shall be placed within the reach of the people. I am satisfied that

this government has not lost sight of this responsibility. The government of the day has done much to place these facilities within the reach of the people and to improve the country's methods of transportation. As to the Intercolonial railway itself, which is the great avenue of trade for the province of Nova Scotia, nearly everybody knows that great improvements have been made by the government of the day in its condition and in its connections. It is a well known fact that, for the long term of office of our Conservative friends administration they were content to leave the terminus of that great railway at Levis, in fields disconnected and separated from any other railway whatever and without any proper communication with any other railway. That, of course, was a great drawback to the road. It is also a well known fact that, very shortly after this government came into power, a great improvement was made by the extension of that road to the heart of the great metropolis of Canada, the city of Montreal. And hon. gentlemen who are familiar with the conditions at the other end of the line, at the town of North Sydney from which I come, are well aware that, for ten long years of the regime of the Conservative government, the terminus of the road there was left at the rear of the town, within half or three quarters of a mile from tidal waters on the beautiful harbour of North Sydney, without any communication whatever with the shipping that frequented that port.
It is also a well known fact to the people of that neighbourhood that the authorities of the town to which I belong were so anxious for the trade of that town and for the trade of the road that they themselves for years paid for the transportation of freight, from tidal water to the railwav station. It is pleasing to the friends of this government to know that they were only one year in power when these conditions at the town of North Sydney were changed, the railway was extended to tide water, a first class wharf was built, a line of steamers has been established plying between North Sydney and Newfoundland, and by the traffic created in that direction the Intercolonial railway has prospered in every part of its course from Montreal to North Sydney. These are a few of the benefits which the present administration has secured, and in respect of which it has added to the usefulness of that road. It shows that this government has not been slow to observe the necessity of putting the facilities of commerce within reach of the people at different points where it was the duty of the government to do so.
I propose to show some other ways in which the present government has done much towards the advancement of those facilities, and after showing that they have Mr. McKENZIE.
done so many things, I propose to ask them to go further and do something more, and to complete in Nova Scotia tne undertakings they have already commenced. I have spoken in reference to that great avenue of commerce, the Intercolonial railway; I wish also to point out some improvements which have been wrought by the Departments _ of Public Works and of Marine and Fisheries in that great system of navigation, the St. Lawrence river. That great course of navigation has been very much improved. We know what it was fourteen years ago and we know what it is to-day. In the maritime provinces we profit equallv as much by those improvements as do the people of Montreal and surrounding districts. We profit from them because navigation is made safer, a better class of shipping can pass up that river, insurance is cheaper, and everything is facilitated by the splendid improvements that are made in that river. We believe that something more is necessary, we believe that millions of dollars more must be expended to complete that highway. In Nova Scotia we consent to the expenditure of these moneys, because, as citizens of Canada, since we share in the development and in the profits which will follow from the improvements, we also consent to share in paying the expenses. We profit largely because of the reduction of freight rates in consequence of these improvements. Freight rates have been reduced from the former figure of $3.50 and $2.50 a ton of 15 or 20 years ago to a minimum of 80 or 90 cents a ton, all owing to the improvements in the navigation of the St, Lawrence river and to a better class of shipping which is enabled to navigate that river. This has done more for the development of the coal trade in Nova Scotia than anything else that has taken place. But this is not the only thing that stands to the credit of the present government. They have also deepened the canals through different parts of the province of Ontario, and wherever else canals have been built, and have made them as free as the waters of the Atlantic. By the construction of that great undertaking, the Grand Trunk Pacific, that masterly stroke of policy will open a tremendous area to settlement, possibly a stretch of country 100 miles wide by 3,000 miles long, which has been thrown open to development to become the homes of happy and prosperous millions. The people who will make their homes in Canada by reason of that grand stroke of policy will not only bring other people into this country, but will bring utilities to the doors of those who have had courage to settle in those parts of the country before that road was built. Many other improvements could be mentioned as results of the labour and wisdom of this government ; these are but a few peaks of


what might be called a mountain range of benefits bestowed upon this country by the wise and beneficient government who have ruled over the destinies of Canada for the last 14 or 15 years. It is pleasing and encouraging to the government, and to those who support the government, to know that as their revenues increase they spread their benefits to different parts of the country, in conjunction with what the great architect and a wise providence have done, as evidenced by the abundance with which this country has been blessed in every respect. When this government came into power we had coming into the strong box of Canada $36,500,000 or thereabouts. We were told then by our friends of the Conservative party that such a revenue was something that was never heard of before, that it showed a remarkable development, that it would be disastrous and destructive for the people of Canada to interfere with this great project of the National Policy, and that the Conservative party, who had brought it into existence, were the men who should carry it forward. But, Sir, the people of Canada did not believe that statement, and they gave the present government an opportunity of showing what they could do. Consequently, we have in Canada to-day, not $36,500,000 of an income, not twice $36,500,000, not three times $36,500,000, but something over $120,000,000 of income coming into the strong box of Canada; and that, no doubt, encourages the First Minister and those who sit around him to spend freely so long as the expenditure is in the best interest of the people of Canada. We find in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific magnificent development at Port Arthur, Fort William and other points on the Great Lakes, and what might be called magnificent developments and expenditures, all in the best interests of the people. No person on the opposite side of this House, no matter how eager he might be to criticise the expenditures of this government, can say that their policy has been other than a masterful and magnificent policy. These, Sir, are but few of the things that might be mentioned that have passed the prospective stage, that are matters upon which we can place our hands.
But we find, Sir, in line with what I have mentioned, that as our income is getting larger, as our abundance increases, as our opportunities develop, the government regards that only as a signal to go/ forward to greater things. We are pleased to find that there is great prospect of further development in matters of great concern to the people of Canada. For instance, there is that magnificent project of the Georgian Bay canal. Of course what I say on this point will not in any way involve the government, of which I
am a supporter, I am merely saying what' people generally are well aware of. From' what has already occurred we may conclude that this project of the Georgian Bay canal is receiving a great deal of attention at the hands of those who are responsible for the destinies of Canada today. We have reason to believe that if this project is carried through it will mean a great many things to Canada, and will realize without doubt most of the benefits which its advocates claim for it. To-day we have strong prospects of deepening the ,/Welland canal, building the Hudson Bay railway and all that follows incidental to these works. With these prospects in view, with these great developments which4 we hope for and expect,1 is it too much for a man who comes from the older part of Canada, from that great little province of Nova Scotia down by the sea, where we have by nature a great many things that require development, to ask that the people of the county he represents shall be placed within easy reach of such facilities as other people in Canada enjoy. Is it too much for a Nova Scotian to ask that people who have been in Canada for perhaps a hundred years should be placed in as good a position as the people of Ontario and the far west? I submit that it is not asking too much and that in asking for it we are not asking for anything but what is a business proposition. In the non-railway counties of eastern Nova Scotia it is well known to the government, at all events, to certain members of the government, that we have ai great many of nature's endowments. We have an abundance of coal, iron, limestone, gypsum, farm and field products and the most magnificent fisheries known to the world. Those are along the sea coast in the non-railway counties, Is it too much to ask that these non-railway counties should be opened so as to put the fisherman and the farmer in touch with proper means of communicating with tliq outside world? I make the statement here, Mr. Speaker, without fear of contradiction, that the farmer, in Ontario, in Manitoba, in Quebec, in Prince Edward Island and in New Brunswick, is in a better position to compete in the markets of Sydney than the farmer of certain sections of my own county and the county of Cape Breton. It is an extraordinary statement to make, but it is true, because when you put your goods on board a car in this province they are landed in Sydney safe and secure and placed in competition with the market. In certain sections of my own county and in the county of Cape Breton, I know farmers, 70, 75, and 80 miles away from the railway without any means of com-

munication whatever, better than a truck wagon, and with this the farmer is not in a position to compete with water and railway-borne goods coming into the market of Sydney.
We are not asking the government to create a market for us. We have it. We have one of the finest markets in the world at Sydney, Sydney Mines, North Sydney and the surrounding country. We have a great iron-producing country, we have a great coal-producing country, we have a fish-producing country, and we have a large and growing population. What we want, Sir, is to be recognized by the government and given such facilities as will enable our people to develop such resources as they have. What we want the Intercolonial railway to do, is to extend its lines into these sections of the country where there is no railway. I think we are not asking too much when we ask that and I, for myself, am not taking too much responsibility, when I tell the Minister of Railways that these branches will pay. When we say that these branches will pay, we have nothing perhaps to go upon but the extensions that have already taken place. The Intercolonial railway has been extended into the island of Cape Breton. If stopped for years and years at the Strait of Canso, and it was extended beyond the strait into the Island af Cape Bieton. We were told in those days that the extension of the railway into the island of Cape Breton would not pay for the grease for the wheels of the cars. That, of course, was, to a certain extent, believed, and for many years the extension of the road into that beautiful island was deterred. But what is the result to-day? I have here some figures. It is not easy to get detailed figures of the earnings of the Intercolonial railway, because a separate account is not kept of the earnings at different stages. But the total earnings of the Intercolonial railway for the year ending the last of March, 1910, were $9,268,239.99. I am pleased to say that for the year, they had a balance on the right side of $623,164.66, a veTy excellent showing for the road. With respect to those earnings what do you think has happened in the island of Cape Breton where they said that we were not going to give them enough to earn grease for the axles? Two concerns in the island of Cape Breton have given the road $989,095. The Dominion Coal Company has given them $739,095, and the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company has given them $250,000 of hard cash in earnings. These are only two concerns in the island of Cape Breton. I might have included its earnings from the Inverness railway, which is quite a concern, the Mac-Kay Mining Company, the Port Hood Company and several other concerns, but these Mr. McKenzie.
are only two from which I received reliable figures. That is only freight. When you come down to the question of freight you will find that these companies have contributed more than one-sixth of the total freight earnings of the Intercolonial railway. This is the freight, of course, collected from these two companies, which is small in comparison with all the freight charges that were paid by Sydney, Glace Bay, North Sydney, Sydney Mines and other large towns which are receiving enormous quantities of freight over this road. The merchants are too numerous to go to them and ascertain how much each contributed. I have simply asked these two companies what their freight contributions were, and I have given them here. The road which is now operating between Sydney and Louisburg is a splendid paying proposition. Of course, I may be told that this is a company road. So it is, but it is a company road that is doing business that it does not want to do. It wants to carry its own coal and any other business it handles is forced upon it. If the Intercolonial railway were extended to Louisburg, it would be a paying proposition. The statement that the extension of the Intercolonial Railway into sections of the island of Cape Breton would not pay, does not bear the test of examination, because we have proven beyond peradventure, that such extensions pay well.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: How many non-railway counties are there in Nova Scotia?

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: The county represented by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), may be well called a non-railway county. I do not believe there is more than one single mile of railway in that whole county. Then, the county of Richmond represented by Mr. Kyte, has only a short piece of road, which is practically no use to them at all. Then, the southern part of Cape Breton county has no railway. The Intercolonial railway enters at the end of it, going into Sydney, but the greatest part of the county may be called a non-railway county. I do not complain about north Cape Breton, which I represent, because we have the Intercolonial railway traversing a fair portion of it, but the county of Victoria which is over 105 miles long and 25 or 30 miles wide, has no railway at all, and is certainly a nonrailway county. I have enumerated for my hon. friend the non-railway counties namely: Inverness, Victoria, Cape Breton, Richmond, and Guysborough, and I think they may very well be described as such. These counties are wealthy in mineral resources, wealthy in their fisheries, wealthy in the products of the farm, but they are hampered and retarded by want of railway facilities.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: And a large part of Halifax county also.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
Yes, that of course, is on the same stretch as Guysborough. I do not want to take up the time of the House at too great length upon this subject, but I want to impress on hon. members the disadvantages which the fishermen along the coast of my own county labour under. Every fish-buyer naturally wants to get the fish as cheaply as he can, and when the buyer comes_ along in the county of Victoria, any time before the close of navigation my constituent must sell his fish no matter what price he has to take, because if he does not sell it before navigation closes there is no means of getting it out for six months and he cannot sell it at all. In the same way, he must get in his supplies before navigation closes and while the vessels are plying to the different ports. Every fish-buyer understands the conditions down there and the poor fisherman is thus taken advantage of to his detriment and loss. But, had he a railway station within a fair distance from him, he could sell his fish and ship it whenever the market was favourable, and he could buy his supplies as cheaply as possible when he needed them. Under these circumstances we in that part of the country have the right as citizens of Canada, as men who are entitled to the benefits of the great development tnat is now going on this country, to come to this progressive government and ask them to extend the Intercolonial, which is the only road within reach of us now7, into these non-railway sections. We need not expect private companies to build these lines because it may not pay such companies to build them, while it might pay very well to build them as feeders of the Intercolonial. Every- railway man knows that a short railway connected with a trunk line may pay as a feeder to that trunk line, while as an independent road it could not live on the bare pittance it would get as* its pro rata of the freight rates, i may say, however, that while there is considerable talk about other companies coming to Nova Scotia and building roads, we are not looking for them. At least, Iy speaking for myself and for my people say, that we prefer to deal with the devil we know than the devil we dont know. That is what I say. We prefer to deal with the Intercolonial which we have and with which we have been dealing for the last forty years, than to start in a new partnership with some concern we know nothing about. Some of those companies are holding out to us every promise they can think of ; they say : Take us in and we will do everything for you. Well, we know that they are not coming their for their health, they are coming there to make
money, and if the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian Northern railway or any of these companies can afford to build private lines in Nova Scotia and majket money, I can see no logical reason why the government, under proper management, cannot do the same thing and do it easier. That being so, and feeling that we have a fair proposition to submit to the government we make this appeal. We ask, as our friends of the opposition asked when the navy resolution was first before the House; that it be done speedily. We heard some criticism some time ago that the good natured Minister of Public Works was toG apt to be granting favours and building public works where they were not asked for and that no petitions had come to him showing the necessity for some of these works. Now, I have here a resolution passed by the Board of Trade of the shire town of Baddeck, county of Victoria, which after setting forth certain facts says :
Therefore resolved, that this meeting would desire to call to remembrance this promise of a railway to Baddeck and would urge upon the government the building of a spur road from the main line to Baddeck, by the government, the same to be from some part of the Intercolonial system, and that the same be built as soon as can be.
I might explain what is meant by the promise of a railway referred to in the resolution. Those of us who were in political life in 1887 will remember that there was a great strife in the island of Cape Breton as" to whether this present railroad would go by the central route, or by St. Peters which was called the southern route. At last it was agreed that the road should go by the central route, but this was only conceded-according to the men who were then representing the island-on the promise being made that branch lines would be built to different parts of the island. That fact is recited as a preamble to this resolution and that is what is meant by the promise that was made in 1887. It was promised that if the counties of Richmond, Victoria, Inverness and Cape Breton would agree to the central route, that afterwards they would receive the benefit of branch lines and that the central route would only be a main trunk line of the Intercolonial for the county of Cape Breton. Last year when the board of management of the Intercolonial were on the island of Cape Breton, I took pains personally to point out to them that it was impossible to serve the island of Cane Breton with one railway. Any person who knows the River St. Lawrence will understand that both sides of that river could not be served by one railway and that is all the more true of Cape Breton which-except for a little connection at St. PeteTS canal-is practically split in two by a salt water lake twenty miles wide at some point. This shows how impossible it is to

serve these two sections of that island by the one railway. That being the case, as I have pointed out to the management of the Intercolonial railway, we are here asking that the different sections of the island shall have better communication, and we believe that when these railways are built there will be plenty of traffic for them. I may sav that the municipal council of my own county of Victoria passed a resolution in almost similar words to the resolution passed by the board of trade of Baddeck, but I shall not delay the House by reading it now. I have already pointed out that one of the great things which they expect to follow the granting of these Tailway facilities will be the development of industries along these lines of railway. We expect the fishermen to produce more fish, we expect the farmers to produce more produce, we exoect the limestone quarries and other things that are essential to the making of iron and steel in our counties to be more easily produced and to make the production of iron and steel cheaper. All in all, we expect to contribute to the alleviation of the conditions which in our country and elsewhere cause the very high cost of living, and to make our workmen comfortable-, haopy and contented. I think there is nothing that would go further in that direction than a reduction in the cost of living. I do not know that the pressure is felt any more keenly in the Island of Cape Breton than in other parts of the continent. Our workmen are well housed, well fed, and generally comfortable; but if we can bring about a condition of things under which they will be able to live less expensively to themselves, I think it would be well worth the attempt, and it would be appreciated by our people, both those who must be fed by the productions and those who produce the commodities which are essential to that purpose. Now, I have presented the facts at my disposal to the best of my ability. I am here, not for the purpose of making a speech, but for the purpose of bringing these facts to the notice of the government, particularly the Minister of Railways, in the full hope and confidence that they will be taken into consideration, and that the necessities of the people whom I have the honour to represent will be looked after in this recard.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
I wish to congratulate my hon. friend on the able presentation he has made of the case, for the construction of additional branch lines to the Intercolonial. The question is one of such special importance to the county which I have the honour to represent, and to the province from which I come, that I would not feel that I was doing my duty as a representative unless I endeavoured to impress the House and the government with its im-Mr. McKenzie.
portance. It is not a new question. It has been up in this House on various occasions, I suppose, ever since confederation, and it will come up again until it is settled, and settled right. It is of course satisfactory to know that all the discussions which we have had of late years on this question have not been fruitless. The government have taken one step, and a very important step, in deciding to lease certain branch lines along the line of the Intercolonial railway. In this resolution we are asking the government to go a step further, and construct branch lines in those sections of the country where no railways have been built.
Every member of this House is well aware that the construction of the Intercolonial railway was one of the conditions of confederation. Without the Intercolonial railway there would have been no Dominion of Canada. The maritime provinces would not have come into the confederation unless they were assured of its construction. [ wish to quote the section of the British North America Act which refers to this matter:
Inasmuch as the provinces of Canada. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have joined in a declaration that the construction of the Intercolonial railway is essential to the consolidation of the Union of British North America, and to the assent thereto of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and have consequently agreed that provision should be made for its immediate construction by the government of Canada. Therefore, in order to give effect to that agreement, it shall be the duty of the government and parliament of Canada to provide for the commencement, within six months after the union, of a railway connecting the River St. Lawrence with the city of Halifax in Nova Scotia, and for the construction thereof without intermission, and the completion thereof with all practicable speed.
Now, it will be noticed that branch lines are not mentioned in that clause at all; and if we are to confine ourselves to the letter of the language, it may be said that the government of Canada never agreed to build any branch lines along the main line of the Intercolonial. But if you look closely at the clause, you will see that rolling stock is not mentioned, that repair shops are not mentioned, that the operation of the road itself is not mentioned. If we are to take that view of the question, then the government would have fulfilled its engagement if it had s'imply graded the road, put down the sleepers, laid the rails, and then said to the maritime provinces, there is your railway, and refused to put rolling stock on or run it at all. If you were to hold to the strict letter of the agreement, that would seem to fulfil it; but would any hon. gentleman say that that was the agreement, or that the Intercolonial or any other railway of a thousand miles in length can be said

to be complete without branch lines?
I think that will not be contended by any one. The system of doing without branch lines has been in vogue on the Intercolonial since its commencement, and it has done more to injure this great enterprise than anything else. Every man who studies this question will know that it is impossible to make any great railway successful without branches to collect the traffic; and the Intercolonial has for forty years persistently thrown away every opportunity of constructing branches which would "have produced traffic for the main line. This unprogressive policy has retarded the progress of the maritime provinces for a generation; and what we want to know is, is it to go on forever? Is there never to be any change? If we are not to have any change, and if the government is not to run the railway on business principles, then it would be better that it should be turned over to one of the great railway corporations.
It has to be admitted that the Intercolonial railway has not been a financial success; it has not paid dividends; but I do not know that we should spend too much time in bemoaning that fact. Those who are familiar with the history of this road from its inception, will know that it was never intended that the Intercolonial railway should pay dividends. When the people of Ontario embarked on this enterprise, they knew very well that it would not pay dividends. If you look over the press of Ontario at that time, you will find that the prevailing opinion was that they were going into an enterprise that would not pay, but would be a constant drain upon the country. They did not expect any dividends, any. more than the people of the maritime provinces are expecting dividends for the $100,000,000 which we have invested in canals in the two upper provinces. It was a contribution to the transportation of the country, and was intended to be so. The Toronto ' Globe ' of the 22nd of December, 1865, just about the time this question was first mooted, expressed the opinion that we were opening an account that would never be closed, that year after year, period after period, more money would be wanted, for it. The Toronto ' Globe ' was right. When we opened the account of the Intercolonial railway, it never was intended that it should be closed. No great railway account is ever closed, because branches have to be built, heavier rails have to be laid, better rolling stock is always required, and in order to get all these things it is necessary to add to the capital of the road. The Toronto ' Globe ' was quite correct when it made that statement. It will not be denied that the Hon. George Brown was an exponent of public opinion in Ontario at that date and he said, in the Ontario legislature, in 1865 :
As a commercial enterprise the Intercolonial has not, I apprehend, any considerable merit. As a work of defence it has, however, many advocates, but if the union of the provinces is to go on, it is an absolute necessity and as the price of the union, were there no other arguments in its favour, I heartily go for it.
The Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, in this House, in a discussion on the Intercolonial railway in 1870, made the following statement :-
Everybody knows that the Intercolonial railway would be utterly valueless in a commercial point of view. It was to be built because they had bargained to build it and they should keep to their bargain.
Mr. Walter Shanly, member for Grenville in 1870, spoke in this House as follows:-
The railway project by itself was not popular in Upper Canada. But when the greater question assumed shape and form after the conference at Quebec, and when it became apparent that in order to bring about the confederation of the British North American provinces each of the parties to the compact would be called upon to make some sacrifice of local prejudice or local interest, then Upper Canada accepted of the railway part of the project as a political and social necessity. A leading politician of Upper Canada, generally recognized as an exponent of the public opinion of the day had said ' Rather than not have confederation be would agree to build ten Intercolonial railways/ That very fairly expressed the sentiment of Upper Canada.
Just let me speak for a moment of the condition of the maritime provinces at that time. Prior to confederation their trade was with the United States. These provinces had then enjoyed a period of reciprocity, and that period had been a prosperous one. They had found a ready market for their products in the New England States, and bought goods from these states in return. They had free entry into the New England States for their fish, butter, poultry, eggs, cheese, animals of all kinds, coal and lumber. All these things, the staple products of the maritime provinces, were admitted free into the United States and there found a good market. Not only that, but the coal trade grew very rapidly, and as ships were required to carry that coal, the Nova Scotia ship yards were busy building them. In this way a large trade grew up between the maritime provinces and the United States which was of great advantage to them. They were then asked to turn their trade into another direction, and it was with that object the Intercolonial railway was built. It was not built to make dividends for anybody, but to change the whole trade of the maritime provinces from the United States to Upper and Lower Canada.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
I submit that the Intercolonial railway has accomplished that purpose, and has not therefore been a failure. While it has not paid dividends, it has done the work intended ; it has turned the whole trade of the maritime provinces into the factories and shops of Quebec and Ontario, and has shut the New England States out of our market.
There were certain things which we expected of the Intercolonial railway. First, it was expected to bind the provinces together into one great Dominion. Second, it was expected that the maritime provinces would become a profitable market for the manufactures of Ontario and Quebec. Third, it was expected that the New England manafacturers would be driven from the maritime provinces and be there replaced by the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec. Fourth, it was expected that the maritime provinces would be able to sell their coal and iron and fish to the people of the upper provinces. Fifth, we expected that the ports of the maritime provinces would be used instead of those of the United States in the shipment of goods from the western provinces.
I submit that these things have, to a very large extent, been accomplished and have been of greater value to the people than would have been dividends. We have, as every one will admit, one Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific consolidated into one great country. We could not have had that without confederation, and we could not have had confederation without the Intercolonial railway. The maritime provinces have become a market for the factories of Ontario and Quebec, and the New England manufacturers have been driven from the field. We have a market in Montreal and some of the cities of the upper provinces for our steel, our fish, and to some extent for our coal. I regret, so far as the maritime ports are concerned, that we have been to some extent disappointed, but we trust these ports will also come into their own when the Grand Trunk Pacific is finished and everything possible is done to direct the trade of Canada through Canadian channels.
I submit that the Intercolonial railway has not been a maritime province road any more than it has been a road for the rest of Canada. It has done more for the trade of Ontario and Quebec, especially Ontario, as it has for the provinces of Nova Scotia >and New Brunswick. That will be proved when you look into the particulars with regard to the trade. I moved a couple of years ago for a return showing the amount of traffic westbound over the Intercolonial compared with the eastbound traffic. I am aware that these figures are not absolutely correct. I am aware that to Mr. SINCLAIR,
some extent they may be misleading, but they give the general trend of traffic The way the books of the Intercolonial raihvay are kept it is difficult to get those figures so as to obtain exact information, but I obtained the following statistics showing the percentage of east bound traffic in the different years :-
1902		 54.03
1903		 51
1904		 48.83
1905		 51-2
1906		 44*32
1907		 44-44
1908		 44-55
During the last few years it appears that the volume of the westbound traffic has increased so as to become a little larger than the eastbound, but prior to that the east-bound traffic was the larger of the two, showing that the Intercolonial railway is really of more value to the provinces of the west than to the trade of the maritime provinces.
We often hear complaints about the deficits on the Intercolonial railway. That is unfortunate, no doubt, for us all, but especially for us in the maritime provinces, because if the Intercolonial railway had a surplus every year it would not be so difficult for us to get those extensions and betterments which we require. Yet the deficits, after all, have not been so very heavy. They amount to about $200,000 on an average each year from the time the Intercolonial railway was started, or about three cents per head of the population of Canada, estimating our population at 7,000,000.
What are the reasons why we have deficits and not dividends? The main reason is that the road has ttfeen run on a penny wise and pound foolish policy from the start. One of the reasons-and one that, I think, is most important,-is that the management have not taken advantage of the opportunities to build branch lines to collect the traffic, even where they might have done so, with advantage to the road. When the road was constructed, they took over the old Nova Scotia railway, which extended from Halifax to Truro, and from Truro to Pictou. And there was a branch from Windsor Junction 30 miles to the town of Windsor. This town stands at the eastern end of the Annapolis valley, one of the most fertile and populous districts of Canada, and one of the richest. Any railway company having the business ability of ordinary 'men, would have extended a railway down to the Annapolis valley to capture the business of that rich and populous country. Did the Intercolonial do that? On the contrary, they let it slip through their fingers. A company was formed, the Dominion Atlantic Railway took it over, and it has now fallen, into the hands of the Canadian Pacific. There was

a chance there for the Intercolonial railway to make enough money to wipe out this $200,000 of a deficit from the staat to the present time, but they did noit embrace it. The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), has drawn attention to the enormous amount of traffic that has accumulated on the Louisburg road between Sydney and Louisburg. That was the territory of the Intercolonial; they could well have extended the road from Sydney to Louisburg and secured that traffic-that also, of itself, would have been sufficient to prevent a deficit during the last twenty years. And that branch might have been extended at a trifling cost. Again, the Intercolonial has done nothing to collect traffic for the road. Why, under the late administration, the very station agents of the Intercolonial, were canvassers for the Canadian Pacific; they gave the preference to the Canadian Pacific, rather than their own. line. At a few places, the Intercolonial touches the sea-at St. John, at Halifax, at Mulgrave, at Sydney and at a few other places in New Brunswick. In those sections, population is usually along the coast. The Intercolonial has never put on boats to collect the traffic as they ought to have done. They allow that to get into the hands of private parties. There is an example of this in my own constituency. The Department of Trade and Commerce gave a small subsidy towards a line of boats which was put on, and is known as the Cann line of boats engaged in the collection of traffic for delivery to the Intercolonial at Mulgrave. And with splendid results- the traffic has grown so as to be very.profitable to the Intercolonial. In 1891 the fish from Canso and these other points delivered at the Intercolonial railway station at Mulgrave, amounted to 162 tons with a value of $11,340, and the freight paid and express charges paid to the Intercolonial made a total of $1,134. Then, these boats were put on. In 1901 the tons of fish numbered 1,900, value, $133,000, freight and express, $19,760. And now we come to 1908. In that year, fish to the amount of 3,372 tons was carried-I am speaking of the fresh fish traffic alone, and am not considering other traffic-the value being $235,000, and the freight and express paid to the Intercolonial made a total of $31,644.03. This shows that by adopting a method of cellecting traffic in boats at points where the Intercolonial touches the sea, a great deal of business could hav# been gathered for the Intercolonial that, as a matter of fact, was lost or went in other directions for lack of facilities. When the Reid railway was built across Newfoundland, the circumstances were the same. The railway touched the coast and on the coast was a fringe of fishing villages. The rail-36
way company put on seven or eight boats to collect the traffic and deliver it to the railway. In this way, they made business for their road. But opportunities of that kind have not been taken advantage of by the Intercolonial, and we can hardly expect results. The passenger traffic to be developed is indicated by the fact that the Cann line of boats carried last year 10,833 passengers, who were taken from or delivered to the Intercolonial railway at Mulgrave.
Now, hon. members may say : What are you asking for? In the first place, we want the government to carry out in the spirit the agreement made with the maritime provinces in 1867. We ask for a complete reversal of the old hide-bound policy of doing nothing, and ask the government to embark upon the construction of such branch lines of the Intercolonial as will give to the people who reside in the nonrailway counties of the maritime provinces the advantage of railway communication. The mover of this resolution has suggested that it might be asked : Why do you not form joint-stock companies and find the capital somewhere to build these branch lines? The answer is very simple -it is financially impossible to do it. The province of Nova Scotia, in most places, is not more than fifty miles in width from sea to sea. A short line, or branch railway of that kind cannot be Boated and financed by a separate company, whereas, as a branch of the Intercolonial and managed from the head office of that railway, it might be a great success. Take the case of any other great railway-the Canadian Pacific is a good example. It has a length of over 3,000 miles from St. John to Vancouver. If I counted them right, there are about ninety branches reaching out to collect traffic for that main line. All these ninety branches are managed by one president and one board of directors, with one head office staff, one engineering staff, one telegraph system, one system of repair shops. All these branches, working together, make traffic for the main line and dividends for the shareholders. But apply the Intercolonial system to the branches of the Canadian Pacific railway. You would have a hundred head offices-or ninety, at all	events-ninety engineering staffs,
ninety telegraph systems, and so on. This fact only needs to be mentioned to show how absurd and impossible the proposition is financially, and that the only way we can extend communication to those scattered districts along the Intercolonial is to get it from the main line as branches built and controlled by the main line, managed from the one departmental office, by the one departmental staff, by the one staff of engineers, instead of a dozen. It is easy to see that that is the only possible way this thing can be done finan-

cially. That is the reason why thinking men in the lower provinces have been turning their minds the last few years to the question as- to whether it would not be better to turn this road over to a company, that is to say, if it is impossible, to get the government to carry on the business on business principles. For my part I see great danger in the transfer to a company and would prefer for the present to remain as we are.
Now we are not here to ask anything that is not reasonable and just, anything to which we have not a right as citizens of Canada. We are asking the government to live up to the spirit of the contract. We are making a sound business proposal. If the road is to be successful it must develop traffic along the main line. The government has adopted a vigorous transportation policy in the west, and the country has approved of it. Now we ask them to do the same thing in the eastern part of Canada. I need not say that everybody knows we have a splendid country in the maritime provinces. The eastern part of Canada is rich in agricultural resources, rich in minerals, rich in fisheries and in forests, yet all these resources are lying, for the most part, dormant, because we have not the necessary transportation facilities to enable us to reach markets. Our people are not opposed to expenditures in other parts of Canada. I do not think it can be said of the people of the maritime provinces that there is anything narrow or sectional about them. Those of us who sit on this side of the House, at all events, have stood up year after year, within the time of this administration, and have voted large sums of money for transportation in other parts of Canada. We have supported the deepening of canals to an enormous extent, we have supported the deepening of the St. Lawrence, the enlargement of that great highway of trade and commerce in this country. We have supported the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the broadening of the habitable belt of this country from one ocean to the other. In addition to all that, we are now supporting the building of the Hudson Bay railway. Now we rejoice at the progress that our people are making in the west, we are just as proud of it as the western people are; but we want to feel in the maritime provinces that we have a share in the progress that other portions of Canada are making at the present time. We are sending our sons and daughters to the west year after year, we have a lively interest in their success and progress. We have ceased to look to New England as our market, and are turning our eyes towards Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, and the other large centres of population in this country, for markets for our Mr. SINCLAIR. '
produce. That is where we expect to do our trading, that is where we expect to sell our coal, our fish, our steel and other articles that we produce in the maritime provinces. But in order to do that we must have an avenue of traffic, the Intercolonial must be enlarged, it. must reach out, into places that have not now railway communication.
In conclusion, I would like to appeal to the Minister of Railways and to the First Minister, and to ask them to deal with the proposal of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) in a broad, generous and Canadian spirit. Let us hear no more of the narrow sectional view that no more capital ought to be expended on the Intercolonial. The Intercolonial is one of the great avenues of traffic in this country. We have already spent over $80,000,000 in its construction, let us spend a few more millions to make it capable of doing the work it was intended to do. This is Canada's growing time; let us do everything to see that not only the west but the east has a share of this development. Let us link up the scattered sections of the maritime _ provinces that have been so long without railway facilities, and allow them to have some part in the trade prosperity of this country. In this way we will be adding to the value of the Intercolonial itself, and will be doing a measure of tardy justice to some 70,000 people in eastern Nova Scotia who have been out in the cold for a long while, and who have been patiently waiting for railway communication, and yet who, during the last 40 years, have paid their full share of the $400,000,000 this country has contributed for transportation in other parts of Canada.

speechtext:
As the building of railways is a matter of interest to every part of the country, I may perhaps be excused for taking up a few moments of the time of the House in prolonging this discussion. I do not rise for the purpose of opposing the proposition of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), because I quite agree with him and with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Sinclair), that if there are counties down in the maritime provinces which are now without railway facilities, something ought to be done to meet their needs. What I wish to put before the House is whether the proposition made by my hon. friend from North Cane Breton (Mr. McKenzie) is the best one that can be made for the purpose of meeting the wishes of the people of the lower provinces. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not at all in favour of government ownership and operation of railways. I do not believe it is possible for this or anv other government that could be elected in Canada to run a railway as well as it is

possible for a properly equipped company to run it. At all events, during the forty years since confederation that this road has been in existence, no government has made a success of it. It is not a success at the present time, although I think the present Minister of Railways is the best, or one of the best, that has ever had charge of that proposition. But the fact remains that the original $40,000,000 expended on the Intercolonial railway has grown to over $80,000,000, for which no return whatever is made in the way of dividends. Of course, I agree to a large extent with the remarks of my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) who says we have derived other benefits, there is no doubt of that. I quite agree with my hon. friend when he says that that was one of the conditions of confederation, and that the government, having undertaken to build the Intercolonial railway, should do everything necessary to make it fulfil the purpose for which it is intended. If branches are necessary for that purpose, they should be built. There is no use supposing that, when the government owns a main trunk line, other railways, or any big railway company which is in a position to handle roads, will come in and build all the branch lines for the purpose of feeding a government road. But I wish to point where I think my hon. friends from the lower provinces fail to take a proper view of the situation. While there is no doubt it was one of the terms of confederation, which I think has been fair.y carried out and in a reasonable spirit, have we to remain under that agreement for all time to come, if some better system can be adopted that will be more beneficial to the lower provinces? I 'quite agree that it would be unfair to adopt any policy or any system of transportation that would not meet the views and wishes of the people of the lower provinces. But I claim that we have now tried the running of the Intercolonial railway as a government road for forty years, we have run it under both parties, and it has not been a success in the past, and there is no prospect that it will be a success in the future. Now if that is the case, would it not be better to face the question boldly, to look into it thoroughly and ask ourselves if there is not some better way of handling the Intercolonial railway than we are doing at present. I would suggest that it might be better for the,people of the lower provinces, and better for the Dominion if that road was turned over to one or other of the large railway companies, even if we only got one per cent interest on the money. I would be willing to vote to appropriate that one per cent interest on that money to pay interest on the sum necessary to subsidize the building of branch railways through every part of the lower provinces which is not supplied with railwsv facilities. If you had a 361
good railway company operating in those provinces look at the change which would take place, look at the new industries that they would undertake, look at the industries that they would start, the opening up of lines, the building of hotels and building up of the tourist traffic from all parts, and more especially from the United States, bringing hundreds of thousands and millions of dollars into the country. The government cannot do that. This government will not do it, no government that you can elect will do it. Therefore, why not put the railway into the hands of a company that would do these things? Take one per cent interest on the money that is now in the Intercolonial railway and it will pay interest on $20,000,000, that would go into the branch lines throughout the lower provinces, and the country would be at this advantage that there would be no more deficits and no more piling up of a huge capital account on which there is no interest coming at the present time or likely to come at any time in the near future.
I am in hearty sympathy with the people who are lacking railway facilities and I think our friends from the lower provinces ought to remember that if the railway were sold or leased to a company it would not take it away from the lower provinces. The road would remain there, and it would employ far more men than it employs at the present time. It would buy far more goods to run the road than it does at the present time. It would be no disadvantage that I can see from any point of view if the road were leased and operated by a company. There is no doubt that any company that took hold of the road -would build far more branch lines than any government will ever undertake to do. If the government undertake the policy of building and acquiring branch lines, if they will not dispose of the road, and I see no other way out of the trouble, it will mean in five or ten years that when these lines are bought or acquired and when new lines are built where there are none today, instead of having $80,000,000 in the Intercolonial railway, we will have well on to double that amount of money, there will be no revenue whatever and the lower provinces and the country generally will not get anything like as good a service as they would if the road were turned over to one or two of the existing companies and let them run it under the Railway Commission as other railways are run at the present time. I would support anything along this line and I would support the voting of any amount of money to build branch lines into those counties and into those parts of the lower provinces that have been suffering for many years for the lack of transportation facilities. I believe that in this twentieth century in every part of Canada where there are people, especi-

ally where people have been living for fifty or a hundred years, it is the duty of the government to see that they have proper railway facilities, but I do not think it is ' the duty of the government to build these raods themselves. I would far rather see them give a large degree of help to a good company to build a road. It would give a better service and it would be better for the people of the lower provinces and for the Dominion all around.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my sympathy with the resolution of the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. Mackenzie) which is now engaging the attention of this House. It is a fact that the people of the eastern counties of Nova Scotia have for many years been under considerable disability with regard to their industrial development and the development of their natural resources for the want of railway facilities. Whether that railway development shall come from the local government of the province, or as a part of the Intercolonial railway system, built by this government; or from any corporation, the people of the eastern part of Nova Scotia, I am quite certain, will welcome it just the same. I find that in the eastern part of the province, especially in the counties of Guysborough and the four counties which constitute the island of Cape Breton, the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway are not as ideal as they might be. In the county of Inverness there is a railway which was constructed by the Inverness Coal and Railway Company. The original charter for that road contemplated that the road should be run from Point Tupper up to Margaree and over to Cheticamp in Inverness. The railway was built as far as the coal mines of Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann and there it ceased. A right-of-way had been given to the railway company for the building of this road by the municipality of Inverness, and from time to time the municipal council of Inverness have extended the right-of-way with the result that the railway stands at Inverness and has not been carried to the terminus to which it was intended to be carried when the Act of incorporation was put through. Who is responsible for the non-completion of this road it is hard for some people to understand.
However, Mr. Speaker, there was a railway contemplated which would relieve the situation substantially in the counties of Cape Breton, Richmond and Guysborough. It is sometimes called the Guysborough railway and sometimes the Halifax and Guysborough railway. So long ago as 1877, 33 years ago, when Mr. Fremain was provincial engineer of Nova Scotia, a survey was made. Here is an *old map of the province dated 1878 and it Mr. TURRIFF.
shows tire line from Louisburg, the winter port, up through the county of Cape Breton and Richmond, through the county of Guysborough and to the city of Halifax. This railway was promised to the people of Nova Scotia under the Liberal government of 1877. Since 1882 there has hardly been an election run in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia, federal, local, municipal, bye, or general, at which this railway was not popped out before the electorate and dangled before them as one of the prizes that was to come to them in the event of the Liberal party succeeding at the .-polls. I find, with regard to this resolution, that I at least am in quite an anomalous position and so must be the people of Nova Scotia because we are pledged this railway extension by the Murray government of Nova Scotia. However, I am quite certain that the people of the eastern part of Nova Scotia will be grateful for the road whether it is built by the Murray government or by this government. I may say, for the benefit of the hon. members of this House that from time to time this railway from Halifax through Guysborough, Richmond and Cape Breton counties, has been dangled before the electorate of these different counties and also of the counties of Anti-gonish and Pictou, because the road would be of substantial benefit to these counties, for the last thirty years. But, to get down to more recent times, to something within the recollection of the youngest of us, in 1904, when the general elections .were on in the county of Guysborough, the local government deemed it expedient to emphasize to the people of Guysborough county the assurance that the road would actually be built. So, with that object in view, a number of wheel-barrows were brought into the county of Guysborough, a few men were employed and near the head of Country harbour they actually graded, if measured foot by foot, a distance of 200 feet of railway. That was a few weeks before the general election of 1904.
