I would ask any hon. gentleman who knows that county well and the towns through which the railway runs, I would ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham): Has the Intercolonial contributed in the least to the prosperity, advancement or development of the business of these towns? Not in the least. Have they had a single advantage in the way of freight rates? Not a dollar. I tried to show last winter that the same rates as were in force on the Intercolonial prevailed on the Canadian Pacific railway in the maritime provinces. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) produced a lot of figures which he said showed that some rates on the Intercolonial were cheaper. But he forgot to tell us that his figures were those of a branch line of the Canadian Pacific on which there was no competition whatever. But, if you take the trunk line of the Canadian Pacific from St. John to Montreal, you will find that the rates are the same _ as those that prevail on the Intercolonial. There is no advantage to the people of the maritime provinces in freight rates on the Intercolonial. We talk about 'the people's railway.' That is a very, very silly _ expression, because the people have no interest in that railway except what they pay for, and pay for at as full rates as on any other line. When we proposed selling the Intercolonial, or leasing it, some people talked as if we were proposing to tear up the rails and burn the ties, and do away with the line altogether.
I maintain that, with the road sold to a private company, we shall have a better road, more prosperous towns, and better accommodation. And we shall have the development of local industries which now we cannot get. In freight rates, I make one exception. The steel industries in Cape Breton do get very cheap rates on the Intercolonial for their products. Is this as a favour to those companies? Has the Intercolonial conceded cheaper rates to these companies to help the steel industry or to add to their prosperity or their wealth? Not a bit of it; they give them them cheaper rates simply because the line must compete with the water route of the Gulf of St. Lawrence-that is all. _ When the winter months come, the officials of these companies, in answer to an intimation that rates will go up, simply say: If you put up your rates in the winter, we are in a position to store our goods until the spring, and you shall not get a ton of them. Consequently, in their own interest and not in the interest of that industry, the Intercolonial carries goods for these companies somewhat cheaper.
The hon. member for Guysborouglv (Mr. Sinclair) said that the Intercolonial " railway is retarding the progress of the

maritime provinces-those are his very words as I took them down. I am prepared to support his statement. The modern company-owned railway not only carries passengers and freight, but its policy is to increase freight, to crdate< freight and to create passenger traffic as well. The modern railway builds hotels, it builds wharfs, it builds steamships, it' creates commerce on the ocean to feed its lines, which the Intercolonial management could not do, which they dare not' do. I say the modern railway builds hotels. I remember not very many years ago in making a tour to Quebec for my holidays, I found the St. Louis hotel capable of accommodating all the tourists of those days. Then the Canadian Pacific railway came there and built a large hotel, some thought too big. It overflowed, and an addition was made; that overflowed,' and another addition was made, thatl overflowed; and the St. Louis hotel, which accommodated formerly all the tourists, was purchased and added to it. I believe this year a still further addition is being made to that hotel.
Now, suppose the Minister of Railways wanted to build a hotel on that magnificent and charming spot, the northwest arm at Halifax, for the tourists who would come if a hotel was there, supposing he came to this House, as he would have to do, and ask for $100,000 to build a hotel at the northwest arm in Halifax, do you suppose he would get a vote? I think there are many members on that side of the House, and some on. this side, who would laugh him to scorn, who would ridicule the idea of this government building hotels for the benefit of Nova Scotia. In my opinion the tourist trade in Nova Scotia, if fitting hotels could be built in connection with the Intercolonial railway, would exceed anything on the Atlantic coast. Nova Scotia with its magnificent summer climate, with its beautiful sea coast and harbours, is the natural playground of all those people north of Baltimore who want holidays. A modern railway run on modern principles would have hotels at Halifax, at Chester, at Mahone, at River Port, at Liverpool, at Shelburne, and a dozen other beautiful harbours on the Atlantic coast, not to mention other equally beautiful spots on the Bras d'Or lakes all around Cape Breton. Could the Intercolonial railway do this? Not at all. I may say that so large is the tourist travel in that province for which there has been no accommodation, that a large and wealthy colony has sprung up at Chester, mostly from Baltimore. There was no hotel accommodation, and they built their own hotels; there, were no private houses for them, and they built their own houses, and every year that tourist traffic has been increasing. A modern railway
such as the Canadian Pacific railway, or the Grand Trunk Pacific railway when it is finished, or the Canadian Northern railway, would have a chain of such hotels built all over the province of Nova Scotia.
Take our local industries, what has the Intercolonial railway done for any of them in the province of Nova Scotia? We have got one of the finest provinces, probably, with the exception of British Columbia, the most promising province in all Canada; yet the Intercolonial railway has done nothing to develop a single industry in that province. It has carried at normal rates the products of the industries we have created ourselves. I remember some tune ago trying to get special rates to develop a gypsum quarry near Enfield, and the rates that were offered me were most discouraging to any business man. I remember a like quarry, only not half as valuable, in New Brunswick near the Tobique river, which did not require any deputation of any member of parliament to ask the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to develop it, because they developed it in their own interest, and have made it one of the most flourishing industries in that community. These are some of the considerations which lead me to desire, in the interests of my constituents, not a government owned and run railway, but a railway that will be Tun in the interests of our provincial industries which for the want of proper transportation facilities, have not been flourishing.
That the Intercolonial railway is retarding the progress of the maritime provinces I am persuaded, particularly in my own county. Year after year the accommodation afforded by the Intercolonial railway in that county has been steadily lessening and the transportation advantages which we once had have been gradually taken away from us. I presented latterly a large petition praying for a restoration of the accommodation that we formerly had, and I have not succeeded in getting it. I am very sure that if a vote by ballot were taken of the members of parliament from the province of Nova Scotia a very large majority would be in favour of selling the Intercolonial railway to any of the large railway corporations. Some may be a little timid about the effect of such a move on their constituents, before they are educated up to the point. For my part, I am not alarmed at the effect it would have in my constituency, a constituency where, for considerably over a hundred years, the people have enjoyed the educating influence of college and academy, where public schools of the best quality are scattered throughout the county, where the people are accustomed to study and to think for themselves. I am not afraid of the result of a vote in my constituency. when the people have thoroughly understood the question. I dare say this

proposition might not meet with favour in some constituencies where perhaps the people have not looked into this question of railway transportation any more than the voters of Drummond and Arthabaska looked into the navy question. But I am convinced that when our people understand what a modern railway is doing, when they understand what the Intercolonial railway is not doing, and never can do, and when they remember that the privileges we formerly enioyed are being gradually taken away from us, I am not afraid of the result of an appeal to the people on the question whether the Intercolonial railway shall continue to be run under the present system. Whv not follow up the question to its logical sequence of asking the Intercolonial railway to build or acquire branch lines? The intention of course is to increase traffic, to increase prosperity. If you will follow that up to its natural seqilence, you would have to ask it to do other things, you would have to ask it to build hotels, you would have to ask it to build steamships, you would have to ask it to go into the business of running a railway on modern lines, as the Canadian Pacific railway is doing, as the Grand Trunk railway is doing, and as the Canadian Northern railway is doing.
I asked some two years ago, the Intercolonial railway to buy one of the best paying railways in eastern Canada-the Dominion Atlantic-running from Yarmouth to Halifax, through one of the finest districts in Canada. It was a business proposition and a good one where no money would be lost and good interest would be paid. My appeal for help to our people, however, was in vain. The question was not even looked into, the road was hot even examined, but the Canadian Pacific railway, with that business shrewdness that has always characterized them, got the road and are delighted that they got it, and so are we. They take possession next May and already propositions are made and work laid out to bring the New England tourists into that province. The present steamers are to be replaced by new ones with 140 foot keel, 2,500 tons equipped in first-class manner for first-class passengers. These are in contemplation if not already under way. Hotels will be built and a proposition is already made to bring English immigrants into that fruit-growing country where land can be got at moderate rates and where fruit-growing is a profitable industry. I do not want to take up any more time. I want to say again that my sympathies are altogether with this resolution, but the true solution, the only proper remedy in 'Cape Breton and in other parts of Nova Scotia, in so far as transportation is concerned, will be when the Intercolonial railway becomes part and Mr. BLACK.
parcel of one of the great transcontinental railway systems.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. KYTE (Richmond, N. S.).
subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I may fairly congratulate the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) upon the happy circumstance that he has now recovered his voice sufficiently to place himself upon record upon this very important question, so important to the eastern part of Nova Scotia, the Island of Cape Breton and to the whole province-the question of improved railway facilities for the maritime provinces. I remember when, two sessions ago, the hon. member for Westmorland, moved his resolution setting forth reasons why, in his opinion, the government should provide for the extension of its railway operations and should acquire certain branch railways connecting with the Intercolonial railway in the maritime provinces, I looked across the floor of the House, but I looked vainly for support for that resolution from the hon. member for South Cape Breton. When the hon. member for Westmorland had, the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and myself to support him, the hon. member for South Cape Breton and others about him sat tight and voiceless and had no word to say in commendation of the policy which was enunciated upon that occasion by the hon. member for Westmorland and which, I am happy to say, is about to bear fruit, with respect to acquiring some of these branch lines in the maritime provinces.
I regret that the hon. member should have felt it necessary to import the characteristics of a barn-storming speech, as it may properly be described, into the debate this afternoon. However, I may say that I was not very much surprised because I recollect my hon. friend had only recently returned from the county of Digby where: his party met a disastrous defeat at the hands of the electorate of that intelligent constituency. The hon. member felt, perhaps, that the speech which he had so elaborately and so carefully prepared had not been given sufficient publicity in the rural sections of the county of Digby and he, therefore, felt that it was due to his determination and industry that the speech should be embalmed upon the records and find a place in the ' Hansard ' debates of this parliament.
The hon. gentleman also felt that it was his duty to make some contrasts with respect (to the attitude of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia in the matter of railway construction in that province. He has mentioned the name of Premier Murray as a person who had promised railways in that province and whose promises had not been fulfilled. It will be news to the people of Nova Scotia when they read (the hon. gentleman's speech, to find that there is

one person in Nova Scotia who is apparently, so ill-informed on the political history of the province, as to commit himself to statements so utterly -at variance with the facts. Since 1896, when the Hon. Mr. Murray led the Liberal government of that province for the first time, a new era has arisen in respect to construction of railways there.
I have always endeavoured to abstain as much as possible from importing into the debates of this parliament, questions which are of a purely local character. For that reason, I must apologize, if I take up the time of the House for a few minutes to discuss what may appear to hon. gentlemen as being -a question which is peculiarly applicable to the political conditions of Nova Scotia, and in which hon. members coming from other provinces can have no special interest or concern. The hon. member has referred to certain railways which were promised in Nova Scotia but he has omitted from his category any reference to the railways built by reason of the policy adopted and carried forward so successfully by Mr.- Murray and his government. I might remind you, Mr. Speaker, of the Halifax and South Western railway, a railway extending from Halifax to Yarmouth, a distance of over 250 miles. An agitation for the construction of that very railway had been carried on by the people of Nova Scotia for many years. There was a time when the Conservative government, defeated in 1896, did take some interest in the construction of a railway throughout that district, but the interest they took was most fatal to the success of the enterprise.
The Hon. Thos. Robertson, in 1894. who represented the county of Shelburne in the legislature of Nova Scotia, was instrumental in incorporating a company for the construction of a railway from Yarmouth westerly towards Halifax, known as the Yarmouth and Barrington railway. He received a charter incorporating his company from the legislature of Nova Scotia, and he went to the United States and interested there capitalists who had the' financial ability to carry on the construction of the railway to a successful completion. He had reason to believe that, having secured a subsidy from the local government, towards the construction of the road, he being first upon the ground, there would be no difficulty in his securing a subsidy from the Conservative government, then in power at Ottawa. Acting upon the good faith of representations received from that quarter, he introduced his capitalists into the province already prepared to carry on the construction of the work, but strange to say, the government and party which the hon. member for South' Cape Breton supports so loyally,
and in whose high praises he has indulged, with such loud acclaim, refused to give a subsidy to the company of which Mr. Robertson was the head, but, on the contrary, they gave a subsidy contract to another company which had been incorporated a short time before, and composed of local men, I understand. The people of Nova Scotia were then edified by the spectacle of two companies undertaking to construct a railway through the same territory -and within a few hundred yards of each other at the same time. Such a condition of affairs could only result disastrously to the scheme to build a railway in that section of the province. But, fortunately, on the 23rd of June, 1896, the Conservative government was swept from power and Mr. Robertson and his company were able to secure a subsidy from the present government to supplement the one received from the provincial government, and thereupon entered upon the construction of that railway and build it from Yarmouth to Barrington. That was the beginning of tlie construction of the splendid line of railway that now extends all the way from Yarmouth to Halifax. The government led by Mr. Murray, was not satisfied with the progress w'hich was made, and he urged the company interested in the remaining portion of the road, to carry on the construction of that railway.
For some reason or other that company was not prepared to carry on the construction of the road, and some time afterwards the charter got into the hands of MacKenzie and Mann, and that firm of progressive railroad builders were prepared to go on with the construction of the road, but they could not do so upon the ordinary terms as to subsidy. In order, therefore, to make the construction of that road assured, Premier Murray, on behalf of the provincial government, entered into an agreement by which the provincial government furnished MacKenzie and Mann $13,500 a mile which secured the construction of the road through to the city of Halifax. Of that amount, $10,500 per mile was a loan to be repaid at a certain stated time and $3,000 per mile of it represented subsidy. But, Sir, that is not all that Premier Murray has done to help the building of railways in the province of Nova Scotia. Down in the county of Inverness there were rich coal mines which would, if developed, lead to an important industry, but unfortunately they were not reached by any railway. Premier Murray undertook to interest capitalists in a line of railway through that constituency, and by reason of an increased subsidy given to MacKenzie and Mann (a subsidy of $4,000 per mile) out of the treasury of the province of Nova Scotia, MacKenzie and Mann, with the assistance of the subsidy obtained from the federal gov-

ernment. undertook to carry through the construction of a railway from Point Tup-per to the town of Inverness. The hon. member (Mr. Maddin) seems to be very much distressed because that road has not been continued from Point Tupper down to Margaree and Cheticamp, but I know of no means by which a company can be compelled to build a railway through territory into which it does not want to build. But," Sir, when a government pledges itself to give not only the ordinary subsidy, but an increased subsidy for the construction of a road, surely that government has done all that can be reasonably expected of it. And, if there has been any dereliction in respect to the extension of that road, surely it does not lie with the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) to charge it up to the province of Nova Scotia. Then, there was a road from Sydney to Louisburg which was built in 1894, and which was also subsidized by the government of Nova Scotia to the extent of $4,000 a mile, and that road is one of the best built and one of the most profitable railways in Canada when you take into consideration the amount of traffic that is carried over it. Again, there is a railway running from Point Tupper into the town of St. Peters, situated in the constituency in which I live. That constituency had been clamouring for a railway for twenty years, and when the hon. member (Mr. Maddin) spoke of the efforts made by Liberal politicians to play one route against another in respect to the extension of the railway into southern Cape Breton, I was reminded of the fact that for twenty years the late Conservative government held the construction of a railway through the island of Cape Breton before the eyes of the electors of North Cape Breton and South Cape Breton, and thus gave to the people of that province an example of railway legerdemain and political black art that has never been equalled in the history of Nova Scotia. However, a railroad was finally built by the Conservative government through the island of Cape Breton along the north shore of the Bras d'Or lake, and thence into Sydney and North Sydney. It is not necessary for me to remind the hon. member (Mr. Maddin) that that is not the most important section of his very important county, and it left thg most important portion of it without any railway. But, Sir, the wiles and schemes of friends of the hon. gentleman were not exhausted, and as late as the general election of 1891 an issue was sought to be made in my constituency by the Conservative candidate of that day exhibiting a telegram through the constituency purporting to come from the Rt. Hon. Sir John Thompson, then Minister of Justice in the Conservative cabinet, and on the strength of the telegram this gentleman claimed he Mr. KYTE.
had received a promise from Sir John Thompson that if the county of Richmond would return him to parliament the government would build a railway from Point Tupper to St. Peters. Then, Sir, the election was carried for the Conservatives, but some two years afterwards a provincial election came on and the same gentleman, who had been returned to the Dominion parliament to represent the county of Richmond as a Conservative, was an active agent of his party in the provincial election. Of course, it was impossible for him to carry out the promise he gave to the people of Richmond in respect to the government building the railway, but in the meantime he alleged he had discovered a capitalist in the United States who would build that railway, and he stated that if the county of Richmond would return two Conservatives to the legislature he would be able to get the necessary financial assistance to build the road as a company undertaking. I am personally familiar with the facts, and I remember very well the Conservative member to whom I refer going through the county of Richmond in 1894, accompanied by the gentleman who was alleged to be in a position to furnish all the money necessary to build the railway, not only from Point Tupper to St. Peters, but through southern Cape Breton into the town of Louisburg and into the city of Sydney. But, Sir, something happened; the road was not built. After the election people became anxious to know what was being done by the company with respect to the railway, and the secret came out a short time afterwards when it was learned through the public press that the very gentleman whom the Conservative candidate introduced to the people of the county of Richmond as the person who would furnish the money to build the railway, had been arrested and imprisoned for stealing $300 from a widow, and that put an end to his railway operations in the county of Richmond.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maddin) is inclined to criticise the action of certain people in his own constituency with respect to a public meeting which was called there to intensify the agitation and demand for the extension of the railway trom St. Peter's into Louisbourg and Sydney. I am not familiar with all the circumstances, but I am aware that a very largely attended meeting of representative public men from the counties of Richmond and Cape Breton attended in Glace Bay for the purpose of passing resolutions calling upon the government to give the necessary financial assistance for the construction of the railway. There resolutions still stand, and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maddin) is in no position to deny the fact that the resolutions passed at that meeting had

something t-o do with inducing; this government to introduce that Bill into the House of Commons last session by which they are enabled to acquire branch railways and under which legislation I hope that at no distant date the government shall acquire the railway from Point Tupper to St. Peter's and then extend it into his own constituency to the towns of Louisbourg and Sydney. In all the debates that took place in this House on thfit question since the hon. member took his seat in it, never once did he rise to give any assistance or support to the agitation which the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), the hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie), the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), and myself were endeavouring to carry on, and which I am happy to say will bear fruit in the near future. The hon. member having held his peace so long, I am sure his constituents will not be disposed to congratulate him upon the stand he has taken on the resolution which was moved this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton North. I should have thought that he would have given his hearty support to that resolution and would have advanced some reasons why it should receive the unanimous support of the House:	But instead of doing so, he has
lugged into this House some of the barnstorming exhibitions which he engaged in in Digby and other counties of Nova Scotia during the last six months. The hon. member also stated that in the past, when the Intercolonial was under discussion in this House, certain Ontario members carped at and criticised the management of the road, and grudgingly supported >any vote of money for that railway, and whined whenever such a demand was made. I presume that the hon. member was speaking for those Ontario members who sit on his own side of the House, for I never knew a Liberal from Ontario to whine or complain about it.

speechtext: I have heard hon. members on the opposition side complain that the Intercolonial was not paying.

speechtext: He does not represent Ontario.

speechtext: I said members from the west. '

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
I have an observ.tion or two to make respecting the speech of the hon. member for 'Assiniboia if I am permitted to reach that point. The resolution moved
by the hon. member for Cape Breton North has, in my opinion, passed the stage when it appears necessary to win support for it. The Bill introduced by the Minister of Railways last year looking to the acquisition of branch lines of railway passed this House unanimously, except for some criticisms which were made of it in Committee of the Whole. If my memory does not fail me, when that Bill was under discussion in the House, the hon. member for Cape Breton South did not rise to give any support to it; but when it reached the committee stage he did make some criticisms of the details of the Bill. There are a great many things to be said in favour of the government extending the operations of the Intercolonial railway through the non-railway counties of the province, but that ground has been covered by other hon. members. I wish to make one observation in answer to the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black), who seems to be an advocate of handing over the Intercolonial to the Canadian Pacific railway. For my part, I have an entirely open mind on that question. What I desire is that railways shall be built in the non-railway counties, and while I would prefer to see the Intercolonial extended to them, by taking up the question of branch railways and building some where none now exist, yet if the Railway Board are not disposed to ad.opt a forward policy in that regard, rather than have no railways at [DOT]all, I am willing to join the hon. member for Hants in supporting a resolution asking the government to hand the Intercolonial over to the Canadian Pacific railway. The hon. gentleman stated that where there is no competition the rates of the Canadian Pacific railway are higher than those of the Intercolonial. That statement he quoted from a speech made by the hon. member for King's and Albert (Mr. McAllister) last year. What guarantee have we that if the Canadian Pacific railway purchased the Intercolonial and thus put an end to competition throughout the whole of eastern Nova Scotia, the Canadian Pacific railway would not put up the rates to a higher point than they are at present?
The hon. member for Soulth Cape Breton also made some reference to the terminal wharf in the city of Sydney, which he said was not adequate to the business transacted there. I am not aware whether the hon. member has the information

if he has not, I desire to give it to him-that during the visit of the deputy Minister of Railways and the board of management to the city of Sydney last year, that very question was taken up by the citizens, and it has since received the attention of the board; so that any defects or shortcomings that have heretofore existed as to terminal facilities in the city of Sydney will be very speedily* remedied,

thanks to the activity of the hon. member for North Cape Breton. I am glad to be able to say that from all indications, something is likely to be done for the improvement of railway facilities in Eastern Nova Scotia and in the island of Cape Breton, and I desire to assure the Minister of Railways and the members of the railway board that every thing done in that direction will receive the approval of the people who are interested, and not unfriendly criticisms, such as those we heard this afternoon from the hon. member for South Cape Breton.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N. B.).
subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of the local conditions sought to be remedied by the mover of this resolution, the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), and I will not take up the time of the House for more than a few minutes in speaking of the principles on which to my mind this matter should be decided,. I discussed this question at some length last year, at the time the resolution moved by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black), in favour of the Intercolonial railway being handed over to one of the great companies was under discussion. There is no portion of the Intercolonial railway in my constituency, and therefore I have no personal interest in the question. But, living as 1 do in the maritime provinces, and knowing something of the business interests there, I think I am in a position to form an idea of what the wishes of the people are. I agree with the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) in the statement that either the Intercolonial should develop the territory which it occupies, or it should be handed over to one of the great companies; and had I been in a position to have decided this question forty years ago, with the knowledge we have at the present time, I am very doubtful whether I would have been in favour of a government owned railway. I do not believe in government ownership of anything if you can have company ownership; but we must not forget that confederation could only have been brought about by the promise to build the Intercolonial railway. That was a compact entered into and carried out, and it must be continued. My hon. friend from Hants says that he believes that if a poll of the members from Nova Scotia were taken, a majority would vote in favour of disposing of the road to one of the great companies. I think he will take good care not to take the poll; but if he does, I very much doubt that he will find the members from Nova Scotia voting as he thinks they will. I can assure him, so far as the members from New Brunswick are concerned, that every one of them would vote in favour of continuing the Intercolonial as a government road, only they would desire it to be made a better Mr. KYTE.
road to serve the people than it is at the present time. I do not believe that any public utility can be operated as cheaply by a government as by a company. But he must remember that while it costs more to operate a government owned utility, yet in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred it will give us better service than a company owned utility. When our hon. friends from Nova Scotia talk about disposing of the Intercolonial, I am afraid they do not understand the conditions existing on company-owned roads. I am safe in saying that the Intercolonial railway affords double or treble the accommodation that is afforded by company-owned roads. It gives us express .trains where company-owned roads would not give us accommodation trains. When the hon. member for Westmorland was Minister of Railways in 1906, he placed before this House a comparative statement ofi the rates charged on the Intercolonial railway at that time, and I understand they are the same to-day, as compared with those charged by company-owned roads, and this statement shows that in every case the former were from thirty-five to forty per cent less for equal distances.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: The rates on the main lines are the same.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: My hon. friend will find that they are from twenty-five to thirty-five per cent less on the Intercolonial railway than on the Canadian Pacific railway. I would rather my hon. friend gave the details. However, some hon. gentlemen during this debate may have an opportunity to give them. My hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Black) says that these companies will go on and build hotels and develop the Intercolonial railway. Well, why do the Canadian Pacific railway not build hotels? They own some 8,000 or 10,000 miles of road in Canada.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: Are they not building any hotels?

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: WTell, they have a few eating houses along their road. There is -a hotel at St. Andrews which they did not build, but was built by another company, and which they took over.

speechtext: What about the Chateau Frontenac?

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: That is a splendid hotel, one of the finest in Canada, and the Canadian Pacific railway have another in Winnipeg, but there are a thousand miles between Winnipeg and the Chateau Frontenac. What other hotels have they got? They have the Place Viger, but it is a railway station. Have they any in New Brunswick? Not one except the Algonquin hotel at St. Andrews, which is owhed by gentlemen Close to the Canadian Pacific railway.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: And the Alexandra at j Winnipeg. .

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
Yes, but that is a thousand miles from the Chateau Frontenac, and they have no other hotel except the Place Viser, between those two points. Let me tell my hon. friend that the number of hotels the Canadian Pacific railway have built do not go very far towards building up a country. If my hon. friends lived along a company owned road, as I do, they would soon see the fallacy of their argument. The Canadian Pacific railway is, in my opinion, the finest railway organization in Canada at any rate, but that company is working for the interests of its shareholders, and is taking out of the people every dollar it can without falling foul of the Railway Commission, and will continue to do so. Any other public utility company will do the same thing. These companies are not philanthropists working for the common good but are working for themselves; and if my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Black) had five years experience of Canadian Pacific railway ownership, he would not be so much in favour of their getting the Intercolonial railway as he is this afternoon. What I contend is that the Intercolonial railway should continue to be a government operated road. That, I believe, to be in the interests of the people of eastern Canada. I know that we are getting cheaper freight rates than we would from a private company. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) says that we have no business to get these cheaper rates. Well, I only reiterate the oft repeated assertion that we have spent a hundred million dollars on our canals from which we do not receive a cent of revenue and are spending a million dollars and more per year on them for maintenance, and we hear of no public outcry against that expenditure. I say that the people of the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec are entitled to what they are getting as part of the confederation compact.
If it be a proper principle to maintain the Intercolonial railway as a government road, then the resolution of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) is perfectly in order. The board or commission which is managing this railway ought, not only from the point of view of good business, but also because they owe it to the people of Canada, to develop the territory served by the Intercolonial railway and make it what it ought to be. The Intercolonial railway is not pushing out for business and I quite understand why. Every time it requires a siding, it has to come to parliament for authority. vVhat we ought to do is put the road on the same basis as a company owned road and get rid of red tape. Let us put the Intercolonial railway
on a business basis, let us see that it is Tun from the operation standpoint just as a stock company road is run. If it be necessary to put in a siding or build a branch line let the board have the authority to do that without coming each time to parliament. There is no reason why this country should not be willing to spend $20,000,000 on branch lines in the eastern provinces just as it is willing to spend $20,000,000 to deepen the Welland canal. I am prepared to vote for that, but I equally want my friends from the other provinces to vote to build branch lines wherever necessary along the line of the Intercolonial railway.
Then we have the principle, which my hon. friend has been so ably advocating for years and which the government adopted last year, namely, the acquisition of branch lines. The same condition exists in eastern Canada to-day with regard to branch lines that existed in Ontario and Quebec some 20, 30 or 40 years ago. In Ontario and Quebec, some 25 or 30 years ago, there were many branch lines built by independent companies, the majority of which no doubt received government assistance, but which were afterwards found not to be remunerative to those who invested money in them. What) was true in Ontario and Quebec at thalf time is true now in the maritime provinces. In order to make these branch lines a success it was found necessary in the upper provinces to amalgamate them with the big trunk lines. They then became feeders of the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Pacific railway and became profitable, which never would have been the case had they remained independent, If it is necessary for the-Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Pacific railway to acquire branch lines by purchase or by lease or by construction, it is just as necessary for the Intercolonial railway. I understand that the government have gone so far as to say that they will lease the branch lines* What I contend is that if it be necessary to get a branch line into a fertile or productive territory, or even into a territory not so fertile or productive, the govern-, ment should buy it if they cannot lease it, and in this way bring the prosperity to the people of that territory to which they are entitled. Go down into the maritime provinces to-day and investigate the conditions under which some of those branch lines are operating and you will see that it is impossible for them to make any money. They have to run under separate business management, they have not the necessary rolling stock, and they cannot get the business. That is looking at the thing from a railway standpoint, But look at it from the standpoint of the shipper, and you will find

that he is compelled to pay practically two prices for his transportation, whereas if these branch lines were incorporated with the Intercolonial railway, he would get the one through rate, and that through rate would not vary, to any appreciable extent, from the rate on the main line,1 because a distance of a few miles does not make very much difference in the' transportation charges by rail. If the government cannot lease these branch lines let them buy them, but get them in some way. Then if there are not branch lines into a territory, the government should build these branches wherever there are people who require them and business to be developed. If the government will adopt that policy I have no hesitation in saying that the maritime provinces and eastern Quebec will prosper to an extent they have never yet sue-, ceeded in doing. We have business there in large quantities; we have many places lying dormant for lack of railway facilities. I believe such to be the case in some parts of Cape Breton. If so, it is the; duty of the government to build branch lines wherever necessary and give those people the transportation facilities to which they are entitled.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
It is not my desire to make any extended observations on this resolution as I have on so many previous occasions in this House discussed the general question of the Intercolonial railway in relation to its branch lines. But I do desire to say a few words that, I trust, will be germane to the subject. I do not understand the discussion of this motion to involve a general discussion of government ownership of railways. If that were the question at issue, I cer), tainly would be very pronounced in my view. But the motion of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) is:-
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived in the commercial and industrial development of the province of Nova Scotia when the Intercolonial railway of Canada should be extended into the non-railway counties of the eastern section of that province.
Now, it is an inexorable law of railway corporations that they shall not stand still. It is absolutely necessary for a road to grow, if it does not grow, it dies or is swallowed up by some other road that does grow. I take it for granted that the government of Canada is committed to the idea of the retention of this railway. Then, if they will have the railway prosper and be of real benefit to the country, they must have that road grow as other railways on this continent that have prospered have grown. We do not need to travel for illustrations. If we Mr. CARVELL.
prefer to go beyond the bounds of Canada, we have a splendid illustration in what are known as the Jim Hill roads. We know that Mr. Hill, a Canadian boy of Scotch descent, went into Minnesota, and he, in conjunction with some gentlemen of Montreal, acquired what was known as the St. Paul and Pacific road, a small line of railway with a mileage of about six hundred miles. The mileage of the Hill roads has grown until it is somewhere in the vicinity of 20,000 miles, unless my recollection is astray, certainly the growth has been marvellous, tremendous, year after year they have absorbed other lines until this has become one of the greatest combinations in the northern part of the United States.
Now, on the other hand, here is the In tercolonial. There are feeders to it, and those feeders are owned by isolated companies, small, weak roads that are not doing the work for which they were intended and not contributing to the traffic of the Intercolonial-in fact, a great deal of the traffic is being diverted from the Intercolonial by reason of the fact that the Intercolonial does not control these roadsr Then, there are sections, m the province of Nova Scotia particularly, that have no railway advantages, and into which sections branches could be extended to the advantage of the community and to the expansion of the traffic of the Intercolonial. These are admitted facts. Now, will the government of Canada-committed as it is to the retention of the Intercolonial-apply business principles to the management of that railway? And when I speak of business principles there is no lurking suggestion in my mind of political as against business principles. If you applied business * principles to the administration of this road, it would mean that the road would be extended, that the feeders would be absorbed, that traffic would be created and the country served by the road developed. A great many are bringing forward the Intercolonial as an illustration of government ownership. The Intercolonial has, never had fair play from its inception'down to the present moment-from either government. When the Conservative party were in power and were etiarged with the responsibility of administering this road,, how did they do it? In an apologetic way. We must remember that the road was laid out as running from Halifax to Riviere du Loup-it ended nowhere. It struggled on ; after a time it was extended to Levis. And year after year as the former government came down to parliament with the estimates for the road, those estimates were put forward with fear and trembling. And the Liberal party felt it to be their political duty to curse these items, and the railway, and the people of the maritime provinces because they wanted, a railway. And now, when the positions of the parties

are reversed and the Liberal government is responsible for the administration of the railway, that tune is being played by hon. gentlemen opposite-they are cursing the railway and condemning these estimates. So,' as I say, the Intercolonial, from its inception down to ' the present, has never had a fair show. If there has been an attempt to create traffic or to promote development, what has been the answer on all occasions? Some three years ago the duty devolved upon me of bringing down to this parliament a proposition for the acquiring of a certain section of railway in New Brunswick known as the Canada Eastern, with a view to making it a part of the Intercolonial. And how was that treated by hon. gentlemen opposite? My hon. friend from South Lanark (iMr. Haggart) an ex-minister and a former minister of railways, said it was like dumping so much money into the sea. And any one who knows the facts knows that the securing of that branch line of railway was the best contract ever entered into by a government in connection with the Intercolonial railway. The prosperous condition of the country that that railway serves today testifies to the prudence of the arrangement entered into on that occasion. My hon. friend from South Lanark, as I have just mentioned, said you might as well throw the $800,000 that this railway would cost into the sea. That, after all, is but an expression of a general sentiment. Many seem to think that money expended on the Intercolonial is so much money wasted ; people have not the proper conception of the work that the railway has done in the past, is doing today and is calculated to do in the future. And? in my judgment, When they bring forward the Intercolonial as an illustration against government ownership, they are not treating the people of this country fairly, and are not doing justice to the Intercolonial. The Intercolonial suffered during the days of the Conservative regime, because there were those in the ranks of that party who were hitched up in their sentiments and ideas with the Canadian Pacific, so that whatever the Minister of Railways or parliament did for the Intercolonial in those days was none against the strong opposition of some within the ranks of the Conservative party, and perhaps within the ranks of the Conservative government. Did conditions change because there was a change of government? I say : No. The Intercolonial railway has been struggling on, and is now struggling on, because there are men within the ranks of the Liberal party, perhaps within the ranks of the government, who are the allies -I do not say in a wrong sense, but the allies in sentiment-of corporations. There is but one alternative, it seems to me, in Canada : You must have a government-37
owned railway system, or you will have a railway-owned government system.
If I were to discuss the question from the standpoint of government ownership, I could point out advantages and perhaps disadvantages. But one of the great advantages of a government railway is said to be that you have full control of it. We talk about how much money we have expended on the Intercolonial, $80,000,000 and $100,000,000 on the canals. But we have got a railway to show for the $80,000,000, and we have canals to show for the $100,000,000. How much of the people's money was expended in the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway? I think I could demonstrate to this House that at least $225,000,000 of the money of Canada, went into that great corporation. I have heard larger figures given; I think one member on the floor of this House, a few years ago, demonstrated, to his own satisfaction at least, that nearly $400,000,000 in lands, money, franchises and rights had been given by the people of Canada to that great corporation. But whatever the amount, if it is $80,000,000, if it is $100,000,000, if it is $125,000,000, how much of that railway do the people of Canada own? You have an asset in the Intercolonial, and the best evidence of it, is that there are influences at work to-day in Canada, almost within the shadow of parliament, to secure the Intercolonial railway, to divide it up as spoil for the Egyptians. Hon. members of this House, speaking of the advantages that would accrue to the people of the maritime provinces if the Intercolonial were transferred to one of the three great railway corporations of this country. I think that perhaps, after all, we had better adopt the idea of having no contention. The good book says that it is better to have a dinner of herbs, where love is, than a stalled ox, with contention. Now, it is said that the Canadian Pacific railway are building hotels, and if it acquires the Intercolonial, it will build hotels on that system. Sir, we have had tie Canadian Pacific railway in the province of New Brunswick for upwards of 25 years, and I would like to know of a single industry they have established.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: A plaster quarry.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
No, they have never established a plaster quarry, or a stone quarry, or anything of the kind. They have great powers under their charter which they could use, but as a matter of fact, they have not used them, and they have not established any hotels. When hon. members get up in this House and propose to decide a great question like this, on the basis of haying a hotel built, in this place or that place, it seems to me they axe not seriously discussing the question. Surely, if



Halifax and Nova Scotia cannot get hotels without our giving away the Intercolonial, then I think Halifax and Nova Scotia had better go out of business altogether.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: Nobody has ever asked to have the Intercolonial given away. We want to sell it, not to give it -away.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend did not say: Give it away, I said: Give it away. But I know something about this matter of giving away the Intercolonial. My hon. friend is an advocate of a proposition made by the Canadian Pacific railway to secure certain rights ,in, and even control of the Intercolonial. How much was offered? It is a matter of parliamentary record that $130,000 was offered for that right. Give it away? Why, if you entertained the idea, they would be turning around and asking you, judging from the speeches made by some hon. gentlemen here, to give them a premium for taking over the Intercolonial. Sir, these gentlemen who represent the Canadian Pacific railway are astute business men, they are astute enough to see its value. The Canadian Northern people are astute enough to see its value. They send representatives to Halifax, and they have banquets and after dinner speeches, and what is the trend of every one of these speeches: How'much we could do for you, if we only came down to Halifax. I do not think they would go there as philanthropists, I think they would try to secure the Tailway as a business proposition. They realize the advantages the Intercolonial would be to them, and they are thereby rendering testimony to its value to the people of Canada.
Now, hon. members having said that the Canadian Pacific railway is charging no more in freight rates than the Intercolonial. Well, freight rates on the Intercolonial are practically the same to-day as they were in 1906. On the 22nd of March. 1907, I laid on the table of this House the tariff rates of the Intercolonial, of the Canadian Pacific railway and of the Grand Trunk railway; not only did I produce the general tariff rates, but I produced the special tariff rates from the evidence of the railways themselves, tariff rates that have been filed with the proper officers. If hon. members will turn to the ' Hansard ' for 1907, they will find on pages 5212 and following pages, the rates set forth in detail the charges made by these respective railways in comparison with the charges made by the Intercolonial. In regard to the rates on lumber by the carload, the charges by the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway ranged all the way from 50 to 111 per cent higher than the charges over the Intercolonial. I am speaking of local tariff rates. I am not speaking of through tariff rates. My hon. friend Mr. EMMERSON.
from Hants referred to the fact that the rates over the Canadian Pacific railway from the city of Montreal, to the city of St. John, were the same as the rates that, prevailed over the Intercolonial railway from Montreal to St. John.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: The Intercolonial railway is 200 miles longer.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: So it is, and the wheels of the Intercolonial railway have to turn around for a distance of over 800 miles.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: It is -about 200 miles further.	[DOT]

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
It is over 200 miles further. The fact that the government are controlling and operating a railway gives the people the benefit of the competition. Then there are comparative rates on coal in carloads. I could give them in detail here. The information is to be found on page 5219 of ' Hansard ' of 1907. The difference ranges all the way from ten to twenty-five per cent. That is, that these other railways charge on the average about 20 per cent more on cars of coal than does the Intercolonial railway on its cars of coal, and its distances are computed from five miles to the maximum mileage of the Intercolonial railway. I need not take up any of the time of the House in repeating that evidence which puts indisputably this truth beyond question, and we all recognize the fact that if this corporation secured the control of this railway there would be the exercise of a monopoly up to the very topmost point which could be reached under the eyes of the Railway Commission of Canada. I could give this additional illustration. The distance from St. John to McAdam Junction is 90 miles. A few years ago, if you wanted to ship a horse from St. John to McAdam Junction over the Canadian Pacific railway you paid, I think it was, in round numbers, $8. The distance from St. John to Monoton over the Intercolonial railway is 89 miles, in round numbers 90 miles, and you paid over the Intercolonial railway $2.90 for the same animal. The people were getting the benefit of that. There is a clear and strong illustration, one of many that I could bring to your notice, if time permitted, but I do not feel that I am called upon to go into that.
I think the Intercolonial railway lost a very great opportunity when it failed to secure the Dominion Atlantic, and I think that the Canadian Pacific railway, with a keen eye to business, having secured that railway, are in search of other railways in the maritime provinces. I know that in my own county the Canadian Pacific railway are to-day negotiating for the purchase of a line. Why? They see the possibilities of the immense development of the shale industry in the province, they see the possi-

bilities, aye, almost the reality of the development of the oil and gas industry in the county of Albert, they realize that today there is developed there and working as a splendid business proposition a plaster quarry. They find their markets in Winnipeg and the prairies for the products of the plaster mines in the county of Albert, and the Canadian Pacific railway naturally want to secure that as a year or two ago they secured what was known as the Midland railway from Windsor to Truro, or, rather, the Dominion Atlantic secured it, and then the Canadian Pacific railway acquired the Dominion Atlantic. Now they . have full control of the section of country from Yarmouth to Truro and of the traffic which emanates from the sources along that line. What do they propose?-crossing over by Brule, getting into Prince Edward Island, putting on steamship lines and acquiring from under the nose of the government railway system a profitable traffic which the Intercolonial railway and the government system secure from Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: That is modern railway business.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
That is modern railway business, and there is no reason why these modern railway methods should not be adopted by the government of Canada through its Department of Railways. My hon. friend, in making the statement that it cannot be done, is condemning our very system of government, is practically condemning all government. It does not seem to me to be a very serious matter for the government of the country to undertake to extend a public work that is theirs to-day. After all there is only a difference in degree as to the principle. If, under the conditions of long ago, it was necessary to build a government railway, and if, during all those years, it has been possible for the government to operate that railway, surely this government, at this time, in the twentieth century, will make no public admission that it has failed to do what other governments have done in this country, what governments are doing in Australia, what governments have done in other countries, especially in European countries and what they are doing to-day. Surely we, in this Canada, at this time in our history, have not reached the point where we are bound to say: Oh, we cannot do it, we must call in the Canadian Pacific, or the Canadian Northern, or the Grand Trunk Pacific. Mr. Speaker, it does seem to me, that if there is one thing more than another that the people of this country have to look upon with alarm it is the increasing power of the great corporations. If you are to hand over this and that government work, and entrust it to a great corporation what is the inevit-37i
able result?-you might just as well put any of the departments of government into the hands of private corporations to run on, the same principle. But, Mr. Speaker, I fear I digress when I speak of that.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: Why is it that Ontario makes its railway pay so well?

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: There are exceptional circumstances. When the road was foreshadowed my hon. friend's friends thought that it would be an absolute and utter failure, but there was a development of a great mining industry up there, they had a monopoly, they ran the road and they ran it on a political basis, more so than any other railway that I know of.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: But it pays.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
They had a very short route, a direct route and an immense business growing up. But, if it can be done there it can be done measurably with the Intercolonial railway. Mr. Speaker, I am not endeavouring to discuss or to deal with this question in anything like a puny, political way. I have no desire to serve any political ends or to discuss. the question from any such standpoint. I am dealing with it simply as a proposition in the interests of the people of Canada. I am dealing with it as a proposition that is brought forward in the interests of a great section of this country. In constructing branch lines of railway the 'government would only be following their own precedent in connection with the canal 'system for the past ten years, because the Trent Valley canal may be regarded as but a feeder to other canals. We are to-day expending large amounts of money, and in the past we have spent millions of dollars in constructing feeders to our canal system. Is there any difference between constructing feeders to the canal system and constructing branch lines of railway as feeders to the great Canadian railway system which we ourselves own? There is one thing which we can congratulate ourselves upon as a people, and it is, that whatever mistakes have been made by all governments in the past in connection with the Intercolonial, we have now reached a point "where we have, I say without fear of successful contradiction, the best railway in Canada today, and moreover we ourselves own it. We have spent millions on the Intercolonial railway, but the railway is ours ; we hav' spent hundreds of millions on other rat ways, but they do not belong to us. I certainly would strongly support the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie). He has presented it to the House with conciseness and with force, and he has given substantial reasons why the government should enter upon the construction of these branch lines. I say, Sir, that the government

should not delay one day or one hour more than is absolutely necessary before they acquire many of these branch lines, in Quebec, in New Brunswick, and in Nova Scotia. At the very earliest possible moment the government should undertake the extension of the Intercolonial railway into those remote sections where there is plenty of freight traffic seeking egress to the markets of the world, and where the people are only awaiting the advent of a railway to participate in the great development of trade and commerce which has blessed all the provinces of our Dominion.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in the enthusiasm on one side for government ownership, and on the other side for company operation, possibly the object of my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) may be lost sight of. I venture to rise to endeavour to call the attention of the House back to what is the real proposition involved in the resolution of my hon. friend.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: Thank you for your kindness.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has so much solicitude about matters affecting the maritime provinces that perhaps he will bear with me for a moment while I treat of a subject which I know is usually distasteful to him. The immediate matter we have been discussing is whether the Transcontinental Railway lines should get into Nova Scotia or not, and in this connection we have to consider the peculiar fact that Nova Scotia is the only province in the whole of Canada which is not touched by the Transcontinental Railway systems of this country.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: What about Prince Edward Island?

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
I stand corrected, but Prince Edward Island of course could not be connected with a Transcontinental line and the correction is therefore somewhat technical. Nova Scotia is the only province in the Dominion separated from whatever advantages flow from Transcontinental railway connection, and we are dependent on the Intercolonial railway alone for connection with central Canada and the city of Montreal. In considering the development of branch lines we have to consider to which one of these great railway systems of the country should the people interested look for assistance and co-operation. It is true that we cannot at the present time look to any of the Transcontinental Railway systems because they have no connection with Nova Scotia, and we have to depend on only the Intercolonial railway which runs from Amherest in the western portion of our province through the city of Halifax and also to the city of Sydney. Let me Mr. EMMERSON.
remind the House that the country traversed by that railway in Nova Scotia is the country which contributes most towards the surplus which for the last two or three years the Minister of Railways has been able to announce to the House. Were _ it not for that portion of the Intercolonial railway which runs through the province of Nova Scotia the Minister of Railways would not be able to report a surplus as a result of his management. Now, what are the people of Nova Scotia going to do to obtain these branch lines? The hon. member for Westmorland tells us that it would be a horrible mistake to permit these Transcontinental lines to go into Nova Scotia and participate in any extension there, and he cautions us to stand by the Intercolonial railway. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) asks the House to saw that this government should pay heed to the call which comes from that portion of the country asking for railway connection. and I say. that the situation in Nova Scotia to-day is such that this government must either listen to that call to build the branches or they must afford facilities to the Transcontinental Railway systems of this country to get into the province of Nova Scotia, so that, if the government of Canada does not afford railway facilities these Transcontinental lines may. I submit, Sir, that this proposition is a logical and fair one. The people of any other of the provinces in the Dominion, can go to these Transcontinental railways and make out a case for railway extension, and they can come back to this parliament and get subsidies to aid in the construction of these railway extensions, and if the proposition is good as a business venture the railway will be constructed. But, in Nova Scotia we have, not that opportunity. My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) may tell us that these companies are terrible things and my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) "may tell us the same thing, but, speaking for a portion of Nova Scotia through which the Intercolonial railway runs, and which, because of the extensive industries existing there, contributes a large share to the revenues of that railway, and a portion of the province which has insisted on railway extension and must have it; I say that when this resolution declares that it is the duty of the government to assist in the extension of railways, the government should either itself provide for the extension of railways through Nova Scotia, or they should give running rights to the Transcontinental railway over the Intercolonial railway so that our province mav in this way obtain the transportation facilities which she is justly entitled to.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. S. LOGGIE. (Northumberland, N. B.).
subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words on this subject, because it is of

burning interest to my county and the adjacent counties. In the first place, I would point out that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), seems to be under a wrong impression, because in the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific there is provision made for the right of that railway to run over the trunk line of the Intercolonial railway into Halifax. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), has told us that the compact regarding the building of the Intercolonial entered into at confederation should be carried out, and in the next breath, he suggested that the compact might be fulfilled by leasing the Intercolonial to one of the great transcontinental lines, if that were satisfactory to the people of the maritime provinces. For my own part, I take issue with him on any such proposition, as giving over the people's Tailway to be managed and operated by one of the transcontinental railways, and I say that such a proposition as that, would not be acceptable to the people of the maritime provinces. It seems to me, that if we are to meet the wishes of the people of those provinces, it will be by our acting along the lines of the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie). The hon. member for Assiniboia this afternoon told the House that the Tailway has not been a success up to the present time. I must take issue with the hon. gentleman in that regard. It is true, the population of the maritime provinces has not increased to the same extent as that of the west; yet the wealth and resources of the maritime provinces during the past 20 years have increased in a very marked degree, and 'the Intercolonial railway has been a great success in the maritime provinces. In the year 1896 it was a road of about 1,100 miles, capable of earning in round numbers $3,000,000. Since that time we have added to its mileage a little over 300 miles, or about 30 per cent, and during the same period its earning power has increased to $9,000,000, an increase of about 300 per cent. During the same time we have, it is true, increased the capital account from $55,000,000 to about $80,000,000, an increase of iabout 50 per cent. So that by increasing the mileage by about 30 per cent and the capital account by about 50 per cent, we have been able to earn $9,000,000 instead of $3,000,000. Therefore, I do not think the hon. gentleman can substantiate his statement that the Intercolonial railway, up to the present time, has not been a success. The hon. gentleman intimates rthat if we leased the road, there would be no more deficits and no more piling up of capital. I do not care very much how much is added to capital account, if we have something to represent it. The hon. gentleman will not object to our subsidizing railways
to connect with the Transcontinental line in the west; yet whatever we give for that purpose, is gone forever, excppt for what we get by increased population, by our own people growing in wealth, and by the general growth of the country. I take issue with the hon. gentleman also, when he-tells us that if the Canadian Pacific railway owned the railway, they would employ more men. Does the hon. gentleman mean to tell us that to do the same work, the Canadian Pacific railway would employ more men? I know not. We know, as a matter of fact, that the Canadian Pacific railway is managed as economically as any other railway in the country, and I think my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, is at the present time, following it pretty closely in that regard. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. iflack), had the audacity to tell the House that the rates on the Intercolonial were as high as those on the Canadian Pacific railway. If he had qualified his statement by saying that they were as high from a common point, where there is competition, he would have been quite right. For example,' the rates from Montreal to Windsor, where tire hon. gentleman lives, are identical on the Canadian Pacific railway and on the Intercolonial railway. From all competing points the rates must be identical. As a matter of faot, these rates are agreed on. But the rates from a given point on the Intercolonial to a point on its own trunk line are greater on the Canadian Pacific railway than they are on the government railway.

speechtext: Is not the rate from Montreal to Windsor lower on account of the Intercolonial being a government railway, than it would be if there were no Intercolonial railway?

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: I would say yes, and I think that is another advantage which the Intercolonial gives the people of Windsor.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: Yes, to the people of Windsor.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext: I also understand the hon. gentleman to say that the rate on the Intercolonial from Montreal to local points is lower than the rate on the Canadian Pacific railway.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL-PROPOSED EXTENSION IN EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
Yes. There was another statement made by my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Black) who perhaps rather took his text from the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), though possibly that hon. gentleman did not mean it to be taken up as the hon. member for Hants interpreted it. That statement was that the Intercolonial railway is retarding the prosperity of the maritime provinces. I am sure that what the hon.

member for Guysborough meant was that if the Intercolonial railway was retarding the prosperity of the maritime provinces, it was because the government were not building the necessary branch lines into the adjacent territory along the .trunk line. There are many villages along the *Qoastj both In 'Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, which have been in existence half a century and are thriving and yet are without railway transportation. In my own county-and I think the hon. gentleman should enlarge his resolution so as to take in all the territory where branch lines are required in the public interest-there is at present, about 20 miles down the bay from Loggieville, which is the terminus of the eastern branch, considerable fishing going on. Thom the stations at Loggieville and Chatham there are each winter about 200 carloads of frozen fish exported. It costs about 10 to 15 per cent to team those fish from where they are caught to the railway station, whereas if a branch were extended from Newcastle, down to Tabucin-tac, a distance of 30 miles, the fish could be landed on the cars at 10 per cent less cost. That would mean that the fishermen would get 10 per cent more for their fish. If a man growing wheat in western Canada could get 10 per cent more for it through the building of a branch line, what an outcry there would be if no branch line' were built. In that case the government would be willing to subsidize a branch line. But after the subsidy is given, we have no asset, whereas if you build a line from Newcastle to Tabucintac, you have an asset.
